p: Henry Ashby is a Londoner, ex Army intelligence, who investigates breach claims for a syndicate at Lloyd's of London.
Eleven months ago he took a posting in Denver to be near his daughter, Maisie, who lives in Boulder with her mother and doesn't much want to see him.
The only person in the city who's been glad to see him is Dot Kessler, a retired federal IT examiner. For nine months of Saturdays she's taught him American audit over breakfast at a diner on Colfax.
She calls him Lime Street, after the address on his business card.
His father, Arthur, wrote risks at Lloyd's for most of his life, and now lives in a care home in north London.
The people you'll hear from first.
Lou Mancuso. A Denver police detective.
Maisie Ashby. Henry's daughter, in Boulder.
Giles Fenwick. Henry's claims director in London, at One Lime Street.
Precious Mensah. The night nurse at his father's care home in London.
Arthur Ashby. Henry's father. A retired underwriter whose memory comes and goes.
Nkechi Obi. An FBI special agent on the Denver cyber squad.

Henry Ashby had been in Denver eleven months and still wore a tie to work, and people at the bus stop on Wazee asked about it the way you'd ask about a cast on somebody's arm. At ten past six on Tuesday, March 9, he wore it across the Brown Palace lobby, under the stacked iron balconies, past a night clerk eating cereal out of a coffee mug, and up to the seventh floor, where a police detective was waiting with two coffees and the face of a man who'd already decided he wasn't going to like this.

The detective was a big gray man in a gray overcoat, collar still turned up from outside, with a lanyard that said MANCUSO in letters somebody had typed with the caps lock on. He held out one of the cups. Henry took it, because at six in the morning you take the coffee a policeman gives you and you say thanks.
Lou Mancuso, Denver PD. Thanks for coming down. Stand right there on the mat for me, hands in your pockets, coffee's fine. Then I'm going to ask if you know her.

It was a corner room with two windows onto Tremont Place, and the sky over the office towers had gone from black to old dishwater gray while he was in the elevator. The bedspread still had its fold lines in it. On the low table sat a room service tray: a pot of tea under a lumpy green knitted cozy the hotel definitely hadn't supplied, a milk jug with a skin on it, and two cups on two saucers. One cup had an inch of cold tea in it. The other sat upside down on its saucer, clean, the way you'd leave one out for somebody who's still parking the car.

She was sitting in the armchair by the window, turned to face the door instead of the view, in the blue cardigan and gray slacks she wore to the diner. Her hands were in her lap, and in the right one, held the way you'd hold a playing card you were about to show someone, was a white business card with a small blue crest. He knew the card. He'd paid for five hundred of them in May and had given away about nine.
Dorothy Kessler, he said. Dot. She was seventy one. She lives off Colfax, on the east side. Lived.

Lou wrote it down, though Henry suspected he already had it. Checked in at eight last night under her own name. Paid cash for one night. Ordered tea for two at eleven forty. Housekeeping found the door on the latch at five twenty and found her. The investigator from the medical examiner's office thinks sometime after midnight. No marks, no mess, nothing missing that we know of. Seventy one, sometimes the heart just quits. He looked at the card in her hand. I'd buy that, except she's holding your card, and I don't like it when the dead hold business cards. Feels like they're trying to tell me something. I hate guessing.
Breakfast. Most Saturdays, at a diner on Colfax. She taught me how you lot audit things.
That's a thing you need taught?
Apparently. I came from insurance in London. Different rules, different words for the same lies.

That was the short version. The long version was that eleven months ago he'd rented a flat in a city where he knew two people, his ex wife and his daughter, and neither of them wanted to see him much. In June a woman in the next booth had leaned over and told him he was holding his fork like it owed him money, and then asked what he did. When he told her, she'd laughed so hard she had to take her glasses off. She'd been a federal IT examiner at a banking regulator for thirty eight years, and she'd spent most of them reading the paperwork of people who moved money for a living. She called him Lime Street, after the address on his card, and she corrected his British spelling into American, in green ink, on the backs of napkins. She was the first person in Denver who'd been glad to see him on purpose.
The sugar packets on the tray had been torn into thin strips and laid side by side. She did that at the diner. Every Saturday, a little row of paper, while she listened.

There's writing on the back of the card, Lou said. Her writing, I'm guessing. We photographed it before we touched anything, so I'll save you the suspense. He read from his notebook. Tuesday, seven. Bring the claim. He looked up. What claim?

I don't know. It was true, and he disliked how it sounded. I investigate breach claims. When a company gets hacked and asks its insurer for money, I'm the one who decides whether the money's owed. I don't have a claim from anyone this week.

On the table, under her folded glasses, lay a manila folder with a red tab. The tab said, in green ink, MC 2018 to 2026. W/P 1. Lou pulled on gloves, lifted the glasses by the chain, set them aside, and opened the cover with one finger. Inside was a single ruled sheet on top of a few more, filled in Dot's small, square handwriting, with green tick marks down the right margin the way she'd shown him once on a placemat. A tick for agreed. A tick with a bar for agreed to source. A circle for exception.
Workpaper, top sheet, in green ink. Finding one. Control tested: the capstone. Result: exception noted. Evidence: see 1994.
A yellow sticky note was pressed into the margin beside it, slightly crooked, as if she'd written it last.
Sticky note, same hand. Lime Street. Check the year. Don't trust the dome.
Lou read it twice. Then he looked at Henry the way you look at a man whose name has turned up in the wrong place. Okay, Lime Street. What's it mean?
Henry looked at the clean cup, the one waiting for him, and the cold tea under the green cozy she'd knitted herself because she said hotel pots lost their heat before you'd finished being polite.
It means, he said, she wasn't finished.
Dot's Workpapers: what an auditor is for.
First, what you've signed up for.
Pull up a chair, Lime Street. Not that one, it wobbles. Get yourself a coffee, because I'm going to talk for a while, and you're going to write some of it down.

An information systems audit is a person with no stake in the answer looking at how an organization runs its systems and saying, in writing, whether the controls do what management says they do. That's all it is. The trouble is in the words "no stake" and "in writing." People hire auditors because they want somebody to say yes. Your job is to say what's true and be able to prove it.

The rules for how we do it come from ISACA, which writes the IS audit and assurance standards in a document called ITAF, the IT Audit Framework. ISACA put out the fifth edition in February 2026. It still sorts the standards into three families. The general standards are about who you are: your independence, your objectivity, your competence, your care. The performance standards are about how you work: planning, risk, supervision, evidence. The reporting standards are about what you say at the end and how you follow up. The standards are mandatory. The guidelines underneath them explain how to meet them. The tools and techniques are examples.

If you hold the CISA, you agree to follow ISACA's IS auditing standards, and you sign up to the Code of Professional Ethics. Read the code. It's short. It asks you to work with objectivity, due diligence, and professional care, to keep what you learn confidential unless the law requires you to disclose it, never to use it for your own benefit, and to tell the right people every significant fact you know that would distort the results if you left it out. That last one is the one people forget. Leaving a fact out is a kind of lie. Auditors don't get to tell it.

How the exam asks it. When a question asks what the auditor is required to do, standards are mandatory and guidelines are guidance. If an answer choice has the auditor keep quiet about a significant fact to protect a relationship, it's wrong.
The charter is your permission slip.

Every audit function needs an audit charter. It's a document that says why the function exists, what it's responsible for, what authority it has, and who it answers to. Purpose, responsibility, authority, accountability. Learn those four words in that order.

The charter has to be approved by the people charged with governance, which in most companies means the board of directors or its audit committee. Not the CFO. Not the CIO. Not the chief audit executive writing her own permission slip. Then it gets communicated to senior management, and the relevant parts get shared with whoever's being audited, at the entrance meeting or in an engagement letter. You review it on a schedule, and right away if the business or the audit function's job changes.

Why do I care so much about a dull document? Because the charter is what lets you walk into a server room and ask for the logs. It gives you access to records, people, and property. Without it, you're a nosy person with a clipboard. When an external party hires you for one job, the engagement letter does the same work for that engagement: objective, scope, responsibilities, access, deliverables.
When I want to know whether an audit department is real, the first thing I ask for is the charter, and the second thing I ask is who signed it.

How the exam asks it. Expect "Who should approve the IS audit charter?" The answer is the board or audit committee, the people charged with governance. Also expect "the charter's main purpose," which is to define purpose, responsibility, authority, and accountability.
Independence: in fact and in appearance.

An auditor has to be independent in fact and in appearance. In fact means you really don't have a stake. In appearance means a reasonable person looking at you wouldn't think you did. You need both. A man can be perfectly honest and still be unable to audit his brother in law's company, because nobody would believe his report.

For an audit function, independence comes from the reporting line. Functionally, internal audit should report to the board or the audit committee, so nobody it audits can bury its findings. Administratively, it can report to an executive for things like budget and payroll, as long as that line doesn't let anyone limit the scope, the fieldwork, or the report. If internal audit reports to the CFO for everything, and the CFO runs the systems being audited, you have a problem, and you say so.

For an individual auditor, independence is about your relationships and your history. Did you design the system? Did you work there last year? Is your daughter's mother the controller? When something could impair your independence, in fact or in appearance, you disclose it to the appropriate parties and let them decide whether you stay on. You don't decide by yourself that it's fine. Everybody thinks it's fine when it's them.
Objectivity is the habit that goes with it. Keep your facts and your opinions in separate piles, and label the opinions.

How the exam asks it. When an auditor discovers a possible impairment, the best answer is to disclose it to the appropriate parties. Watch for choices that have the auditor quietly withdraw, quietly continue, or ask the auditee for permission.

You will never have time to audit everything. Nobody does. So you plan by risk. Start with the audit universe, the full list of systems, processes, and units you could audit. Assess the risk of each one, using data where you have it and judgment where you don't, and spend your hours where the risk is highest. That gives you the long term plan and the plan for this year, and the audit committee should agree to both.

When you plan a single engagement, you write down the areas to be audited, the objectives, the scope, the criteria you'll measure against, the resources and dates, the deliverables, how you'll communicate and escalate, and what technology and data analysis you'll use. A plan that only lives in your head isn't a plan. It's a mood.

Audit risk is the risk that you reach the wrong conclusion. It has three parts. Inherent risk is how likely an area is to have a material error before any controls, just because of what it is: a payment system moving billions a day has more inherent risk than the cafeteria menu. Control risk is the chance the controls won't prevent or catch that error in time. Detection risk is the chance your own procedures miss it. You can't change the first two. You can change the third, by doing more testing, better testing, or testing of the right things. When inherent and control risk are high, you need more evidence to keep audit risk low.

Materiality is your threshold for what matters. Set it in planning, and know that it's professional judgment, not a formula you look up. The lower you set it, the more precise you have to be, and the more evidence you'll need. A good auditor can tell you why her materiality is what it is.

How the exam asks it. "Which component of audit risk can the auditor control?" Detection risk. "What happens when the materiality threshold is lowered?" You need more or more precise testing. Risk-based planning questions want the answer that puts effort where risk is highest.

Your conclusions are only as good as your evidence, and the standard is sufficient and appropriate. Sufficient is about quantity: is there enough? Appropriate is about quality: is it relevant and reliable? You evaluate that with professional skepticism, which is a polite word for checking.

Some evidence is better than other evidence. From weakest to strongest, by how you got it: asking someone, watching them, inspecting documents and records, recalculating it yourself, and doing the procedure again yourself, which we call re-performance. Analytical procedures, comparing numbers against each other or against what you'd expect, are good at telling you where to look, and then you go and look. Written beats oral. Evidence you obtain directly beats evidence the auditee hands you. Evidence from an independent source beats evidence from the people whose work you're checking. A bank's confirmation of a balance beats the company's spreadsheet of the same balance. And a nice man telling you it's all fine is the bottom of the pile, however nice he is.

Keep your evidence, and protect it. Your workpapers have to show what you did, what you found, and how you got from one to the other, so another competent auditor could follow the trail without phoning you. Retain them as long as policy and law say, and keep them safe from anyone who'd like to change them.

If evidence might end up in a legal proceeding, talk to counsel before you collect it, because the rules for how it's gathered, handled, and handed over get stricter. That's where you hear about chain of custody: who had it, when, and what they did with it, from the moment you found it. Break that chain, and the best evidence in the world turns into an argument.

And when you find signs of irregularities or illegal acts, you document them and tell the appropriate party in a timely manner. Not your friend. Not the person you suspect. The party whose job it is to act.

How the exam asks it. Reliability questions want independent, written, directly obtained evidence, and re-performance over inquiry. If an answer has the auditor confront the suspect or alert the auditee before protecting evidence and notifying the right party, it's wrong.

Lou's radio muttered on his shoulder. He listened, said Coming, and pointed at the carpet in front of Henry's shoes. Medical investigator's van. I'm going to be ninety seconds. You stay there. You don't touch anything. That includes the coffee you're holding, which you can't put down. The door clicked shut behind him.

Henry stood where he'd been put. From the doorway he could see the folder's top sheet, and beneath it the corner of a second sheet that had slipped a quarter inch out of line. On that corner, in the same green ink, was W/P 17 and half a word that might have been LATT.
Somewhere down the hall a vacuum started up and stopped again. Nobody had moved Dot's glasses since Lou put them down. They sat folded by the teapot with the chain in a little heap next to them.
Left alone at a death scene, Henry can almost read Dot's working papers. What should he do?
A. Step over and nudge the top sheet aside with his pen to read the page under it.
B. Ease his own card out of Dot's fingers before anybody else handles it.
C. Photograph the visible pages on his phone from the doorway without moving.
D. Stay where he is and ask Lou to photograph the shifted page when he's back.

Lou comes back with a medical investigator in a blue windbreaker, and Henry tips his head at the folder before either of them can tell him to move. Second sheet's slipped out from under the first. You'll want it before anybody touches it. Lou gives him the look you'd give a dog that's fetched the right newspaper, then calls the crime scene tech back in. She photographs every page exactly where it lies, bags the folder, and writes 6:31 on a clipboard with a pen tied to it by a bit of string, which Henry finds oddly reassuring. I'll get you copies once the lab has it, Lou says. It's a better offer than anything Lou had made at ten past six.

Tick, agreed to source. Preserve first, document second, and let the person responsible for the evidence collect it. Pointing out what you saw is helpful. Touching it is a problem. A photograph in place, a log entry, and a time make the evidence usable later.
When the medical investigator had gone back down to her van, Lou came and leaned on the door frame next to Henry and drank his coffee, which must have been stone cold by then, as if it was fine.
You investigate for a living, he said. So investigate. Tell me what you see. I'll tell you if it's useful.
A. "Somebody she trusted came up for tea last night, and she died after they left."
B. "She examined banks for thirty eight years. Plenty of people disliked her."
C. "Nothing useful yet. I'd want the toxicology back from the lab before I guess."
D. "Two cups, one used and one clean. She was expecting somebody. I can't say who."

He starts with what's on the table. Two cups, one used and one clean. She was expecting somebody. I can't say who. Then he adds the rest. She's torn the sugar packets into strips, which she did at the diner whenever she was waiting on somebody, and she's turned the chair round to face the door instead of the window. I'd say she was expecting a person, probably me, at seven. That bit's a guess. Lou writes all of it down, guess included, and underlines something. Okay, he says after a moment. That I can use.

That's the one, Lime Street. That's objectivity in practice. You list what you directly observed, you offer an inference and label it as one, and you say what you don't know. Directly observed facts carry more weight than anyone's theory, including yours.
In the corridor, by a window that looked down past the iron balconies to the lobby, he finally listened to the voicemail he'd seen at 5:40 and had been too busy getting his trousers on to play.

Voicemail, Monday, 11:48 PM. Lime Street. It's Dot. I know it's late, go back to sleep after this. I'm at the Brown Palace, don't laugh, I wanted one good bed in my life. Come at seven. They're filing in the morning and you're going to get it, and I want you to have my papers before you read a word of theirs. Bring a pen. Bring two. Goodnight.
He played it twice. Then he saw the other notification, the one under it. A missed call at 6:47 from Maisie. And a text, two minutes later.
A text from Maisie. never mind
Maisie was fourteen. She hadn't rung him in six weeks. It was 7:05, and the school bus in Boulder came at half past.
Maisie rang at 6:47 and then texted never mind. What should Henry do?
A. Ring her now and tell her everything: the hotel, the police, the card.
B. Ring her back now, and tell her plainly that a friend of his died.
C. Text her that he's stuck at work and will ring her tonight.
D. Wait and ring her this evening, once her school day is over.

She picks up on the fourth ring. Hi. He tells her, in two sentences, with nothing dressed up. There's a pause. Oh. Sorry. Was it the diner lady? He hadn't known she knew about the diner lady. Mum said to ask if you want to come to the science fair. It's Thursday. Six. You don't have to. I'll be there. K. She hangs up. A minute later: its on benfords law. about how to catch people lying with numbers. you'd probably like it.

Good. Write it down. Timely, honest, and pitched to the person you're talking to. That's the whole of good communication, in audit reports and with fourteen year olds. Short and true beats complete and late.

His office was two rooms above a bicycle shop on Wazee Street in LoDo, with a brass plate on the door that the landlord had called "a choice." He was hanging up his coat at 9:06 when the email came in, and at 9:10 his phone rang with a London number.

An email from Vellacott Claims, One Lime Street. Subject: NEW CLAIM: Meridian Clearing, Inc. Cyber policy, notice of loss. Insured: Meridian Clearing, Inc., Denver, Colorado (payment processing and settlement). Event: Ransomware and unauthorized access, discovered Friday, March 5, 2027, 4:40 AM local. Amount claimed: US$300,000,000 (policy limit). Prior regulatory examinations of insured's IT, disclosed per proposal form: federal banking regulator, 2018 to 2026. Examiner in charge: D. Kessler. Assigned: H. Ashby.

Henry. It's Giles. You've seen it? Three hundred million, the whole limit, and the reinsurers are already ringing. It's yours. You're the only one of us in the same time zone as the damage. Giles Fenwick, claims director, said it the way he said everything, as though he'd just come in from a brisk walk.
Henry read the line about prior examinations again. D. Kessler. Nine years. MC 2018 to 2026. Bring the claim.
The claim names Dot as the insured's examiner for nine years, and Henry knew her. What should he do?
A. Accept the claim and keep his friendship with Dot to himself.
B. Tell Giles about his friendship with Dot and let London decide.
C. Accept, and have a London colleague sign the reports in his place.
D. Turn the claim down himself, given the card in Dot's hand.

He tells it straight: the diner, the card, the voicemail, the folder in police custody. Giles is quiet for longer than Giles is usually quiet. Right. Put that in writing to me and to compliance within the hour. If they're content, it stays yours, and the note goes on the file. At ten to ten compliance replies: content, with disclosure recorded. It's the first thing all day that feels like solid ground.

Tick, agreed to source. When something might impair your independence, in fact or in appearance, you disclose it to the appropriate parties and let them decide. Then you document it. That protects the work, the people relying on it, and you.

Now, don't overthink it, Giles said. Pop down to Meridian this afternoon, have a poke about, see what they've got, and give me a view by Friday. The board will ask on Monday and I'd like to have something better than a shrug.
Friday was three days away. The claim was the size of a small country's defense budget. Henry looked at the whiteboard on his office wall, which still had a shopping list on it.
Giles wants a view on a $300 million claim by Friday. What should Henry do first?
A. Write a one page plan for the work before he asks Meridian for anything.
B. Send Meridian's broker every document request he can think of today.
C. Tell Giles that Friday is impossible and he'll report when the work's done.
D. Drive to Meridian's office this afternoon and ask what they'll show him.

The plan takes forty minutes. Objective: decide whether the loss is covered and in what amount. Scope: the March 5 event and the losses claimed. Criteria: the policy wording. A short, ranked request list. Dates, with Friday as an interim view, not an opinion. Escalation: Giles, then counsel. He sends it to Giles at 10:35. Good Lord, a plan, Giles writes back. Approved.

That's the one, Lime Street. That's engagement planning: objectives, scope, criteria, resources, timeline, deliverables, and how you'll communicate and escalate. A written plan also manages expectations. A Friday view is achievable. A Friday opinion on a 300 million dollar claim isn't.

The claim pack arrived at 11:34 from Meridian's broker, as a single PDF of 412 pages and a spreadsheet. Henry printed the summary page, because he thought better on paper and because Dot had once told him a man who reads loss figures on a screen is a man who'll believe them.

Meridian Clearing, claim summary (insured's figures). Business interruption, 9 days, estimated: $182,000,000. Restoration and forensic costs: $52,000,000. Fraudulent settlements during the event: $41,000,000. Third party liability, merchant claims: $25,000,000. Total claimed: $300,000,000 (policy limit; amounts above limit not shown)
Supporting documents ran from page 5 to page 412 and were in no particular order. He had three days.
Which part of Meridian's loss summary deserves Henry's attention first?
A. Start with the smallest item, the merchant liability claims.
B. Start with the forensic firm's summary and adopt its figures.
C. Start on page 5 and read straight through to page 412 in order.
D. Start with the $182 million business interruption estimate.

He circles business interruption. It's an estimate, built by Meridian's own finance team, from Meridian's own assumptions about what the nine days would have earned. High value, high judgment, and high chance of a generous error. The fraud losses come second: smaller, but they should be backed by transaction data he can test himself. He writes the order on the whiteboard, under the shopping list.

Good. Write it down. That's risk-based planning. Rank the areas by how much they're worth and how likely they are to be wrong. An estimate built by the claimant carries high inherent risk. Put your hours there first.
At 12:15 an email arrived from Meridian's director of internal audit, a man named Leonard Pratt, who had evidently been told an investigator had been assigned and had decided to get ahead of it.

An email from Leonard Pratt, Director, Internal Audit, Meridian Clearing. Subject: Saving you some time. Mr. Ashby, welcome aboard. Attached is our 2026 IT general controls report, signed off by our CFO, Carla Wynn, to whom I report. Conclusion: controls effective, no significant findings. Happy to walk you through it so you don't have to reinvent the wheel. Best, Leonard.
Henry read to whom I report three times. Dot used to say that the most important line in any audit report is the one about who the auditor works for, and that it's usually in the smallest type.
Leonard Pratt, who reports to the CFO, offers internal audit's clean ITGC report. What should Henry do with it?
A. Set the report aside and plan his testing as if it didn't exist.
B. Take the report at face value and scale back his own testing to match.
C. Ask for the charter and the workpapers before deciding how far to rely.
D. Ask Leonard to confirm in writing that his conclusion still stands.

Leonard sends the charter within the hour. It's signed by Carla Wynn, CFO. There's no audit committee approval on it anywhere. Leonard's workpapers will take "a little longer." Henry writes in his own notes: IA reports to CFO for all purposes. Charter not approved by those charged with governance. Reliance: limited, pending review.

Tick, agreed to source. Before you rely on another auditor's work, check the foundations. The charter should be approved by those charged with governance, and the function's reporting line should protect it from undue influence. Then review the work itself and document how much you'll rely on it.
Decision eight. Eight o'clock in Muswell Hill.

At one o'clock his phone showed a London number he knew by heart. It was eight in the evening at Elmcroft, the care home in Muswell Hill where his father had lived since the autumn, and the night nurse, Precious, always rang at eight on Tuesdays because Arthur did better before the evening news.
He's had a good day, Henry. He's been asking for you. I'll hold the phone, he keeps dropping it.

Then his father's voice, the big Lloyd's voice that used to fill the Room in the seventies, thinner now. They rang the Lutine today. Twice. Good news. Somebody's ship came home. A pause. Henry could hear a television. Did Dorothy find you? The American girl. With the red folder. She said she'd keep an eye on you.
Henry sat down on the edge of his desk, quite slowly.
A. Ask him one open question about her and write his words down afterward.
B. Press him for dates and names now, while he still seems clear.
C. Ask Precious whether anyone called Dorothy has rung or visited lately.
D. Gently correct him about the bell and tell him he doesn't know a Dorothy.

Tell me about her, Dad. Clever. Terrible tea. She came to the Room about the Denver risk. Ninety four. I put a line on it, you know. My last big line. Then the news comes on, and his father wants to watch it. After the call Henry writes it all down, word for word, with the time, and under it: source reliability low, corroborate. Then he sits for a while with his hand over his mouth.

That's the one, Lime Street. Inquiry is the weakest kind of evidence, and a source with dementia is about as unreliable as sources get. It's still evidence. Capture it accurately, label its reliability honestly, and go looking for something independent that agrees. And be his son first.
Decision nine. The control that failed.

Meridian's own account of the attack, on page 31, was confident. An intruder using an administrator's account had got past the dual authorization on outgoing settlement files, and 41 million dollars in fraudulent settlements had gone out over three days before anyone noticed.
Dual authorization: two people must approve before a file goes out. The claim pack called it Meridian's key control, and said it had failed. Dot's top sheet had a shorter name for it. The capstone.
Henry thought about the three days. Three days was a long time for 41 million dollars to be missing from a company whose whole business was knowing where money was.
Meridian says an intruder beat dual authorization, and fraud ran for three days. What should Henry check first?
A. Accept that the intruder beat the key control and move on to the losses.
B. Ask for the daily settlement reconciliations for that whole week.
C. Review the dual authorization settings and approval records for those days.
D. Recommend that Meridian add more preventive controls on settlement files.

If the preventive control was beaten, the detective control should still have fired: every morning, Meridian reconciles what it settled against what the Federal Reserve says it settled. Three mornings, three chances. He adds it to the top of the request list: daily reconciliations, March 2 to 5, with sign-offs. Either they flagged the fraud and somebody ignored them, or they didn't run.

Good. Write it down. Preventive controls stop problems. Detective controls find the ones that got through. Corrective controls fix the damage. When a preventive control fails, test the detective control behind it. A three day gap points at the reconciliation.

At 3:30 someone knocked on the brass plate, which nobody had ever done. The woman on the landing was about forty, in a navy parka, with an FBI credential she held up long enough for him to read it properly, which he did.

Special Agent Nkechi Obi, Denver field office, cyber squad. Meridian Clearing reported its ransomware to us on Friday. This morning a Denver detective called to say a retired bank examiner died holding your card, with a folder marked MC. So here I am. She looked around the office, at the whiteboard and the shopping list. I'd like your claim file, and anything Ms. Kessler sent you. Informally. Today.
A. Offer her the claim file in exchange for what the FBI has on Meridian.
B. Refuse to share anything until she comes back with a subpoena.
C. Give her Dot's voicemail, and send the claim file through counsel.
D. Hand over the whole claim file now and sort out the paperwork later.

He plays her the voicemail and sends it to her, and tells her about the card, the folder, and the clean cup. For the claim file, he calls Vellacott's American counsel while she listens, and counsel asks for a written request. Agent Obi nods as if that's the answer she expected. You'll be hearing from us formally, she says. Thanks for the voicemail. That's the most useful thing anyone's given me today.

Tick, agreed to source. Share what you lawfully can, promptly. Route your client's confidential information through the process the law and your engagement require, which usually means counsel and a formal request. That's due care and confidentiality working together, and it keeps the evidence admissible.
Decision eleven. Twelve thousand four hundred.

By seven the office smelled of reheated noodles. The claim spreadsheet held the settlements Meridian said were fraudulent: 12,400 rows, one for each payment, with an amount, a date and time, a destination account, and a merchant code. The total at the bottom said $41,000,000.
Meridian's forensic firm had "validated" the list by reviewing 25 of them.
How should Henry test Meridian's list of fraudulent settlements?
A. Query all the rows for odd patterns, then sample the ones flagged.
B. Pull a random sample of 60 settlements and trace each one by hand.
C. Accept the forensic firm's validation of the 25 rows it reviewed.
D. Test the 25 largest settlements in detail and trace each to source.

Three short queries in the free database tool he keeps for exactly this. No duplicates. Most of the payments went out between two and four in the morning, Denver time, when nobody at Meridian would be at a desk. Then something he doesn't like at all: 2,906 of them sit between $9,000 and $9,999, just under the $10,000 line where Meridian's second approver is supposed to look. Whoever chose those amounts knew where the line was. He writes it down with the query beside it and circles it.

That's the one, Lime Street. Data analytics, sometimes called CAATs, let you test the entire population instead of a slice of it. Use them to find the patterns, then sample the flagged items for detailed vouching. Amounts that cluster just under an approval limit are a classic red flag.
At 8:10 his phone buzzed on the desk.
A text from Lou. Medical examiner's prelim. Time of death between midnight and 1:30. No cause yet, tox in two weeks. That stays with you.

Henry wrote the times on the whiteboard, under the order of work and the shopping list, and went back to the claim pack. At 9:40, on page 388, he reached Appendix C. Meridian had attached it to show the intruder's movements. It listed every outside account that could reach Meridian's systems, and every sign in since March 1, with the times in UTC. The export had been run that morning, a few hours before the broker sent the pack.
He typed KESSLER into the search box. He told himself it was thoroughness.

Claim pack, Appendix C, page 388. Account E X T zero four one two, Dorothy Kessler, federal banking regulator, examiner, read only. Access granted April 2, 2018. Access end, November 30, 2026. Status, active. Then two lines from March 9, 2027. At ten twelve and thirty seven seconds UTC, the account signs in to the examiner portal. At ten forty one, it signs out.

Ten twelve UTC was 3:12 in the morning in Denver. By the medical investigator's reckoning, Dot had been dead for at least an hour and a half by then, in an armchair at the Brown Palace, facing the door. And her account, which should have been switched off in November when her last examination closed, had signed in to Meridian's examiner portal and stayed for twenty eight minutes.

He didn't know who. He had no idea what they'd looked at. It was 9:47 on a Tuesday night, and he was holding evidence in a death and in a 300 million dollar claim at the same time, and neither one was his.
Appendix C shows Dot's account signing in hours after she died. What should Henry do with it?
A. Email Leonard Pratt tonight and ask why Dot's account signed in.
B. Ring Lou now and read him the two log lines over the phone.
C. Preserve the log as received and get it to Lou through counsel tonight.
D. Hold it for Friday's interim view and send it with everything else.

He saves the pack exactly as the broker sent it and writes down the page, the email that delivered it, the time he opened Appendix C, and the file's checksum. After that he doesn't touch the original. Then he rings Vellacott's American counsel at home. She listens, asks two questions, and at 10:31 sends the extract to Lou and Agent Obi under a cover letter that says where it came from and who has held it. Obi replies at 10:40. Received. Don't raise it with Meridian. He hadn't planned to. He copies Giles, who's asleep, so it's the first thing he reads.

Good. Write it down. When you find signs of an illegal act, preserve the evidence as you received it, record its source and handling, and report it promptly to the party whose job it is to act, through the channel your engagement requires. The speed matters and so does the route. That's what keeps one log line usable as evidence.
At 11:15 the office was quiet except for the bicycle shop's freezer humming through the floor. Meridian didn't know what he'd seen. For one night, that felt like the only advantage he had.

He tore a sheet off the pad and did what Dot would have done. Date at the top: Tuesday, March 9, 2027. Then the day in order, with nothing improved. The room. The card. The folder in police custody. The notice and the disclosure. Leonard's charter, with the CFO's signature on it and nobody else's. His father's words, with the reliability written underneath. 2,906 settlements just under a line. An account that should have been closed in November, signing in after its owner had died.
At the bottom, in the space she'd taught him to leave for it, he wrote the conclusion. Exception noted. It was the only thing he was sure of.
His phone lit up at 11:40. Maisie, who was supposed to be asleep.

A text from Maisie. ok so if you take the first digit of a ton of real numbers like town populations or electric bills, 1 comes up like 30% of the time and 9 hardly ever. when people make numbers up they come out too even. thats how you catch them
A text from Maisie. anyway night

He looked at the claim spreadsheet, still open on the other screen. Twelve thousand four hundred first digits. Night, he wrote back. Can I borrow your project? Three dots appeared, went away, and came back. only if you come thursday

By any fair standard it had been a careful day, and that was what bothered him. He'd done the work properly, and a dead woman's account had still signed in to a payment company at 3:12 in the morning.
Before he turned off the lamp he went back to page 31, where Meridian described the attack, and found a sentence he'd skimmed at lunch.
Claim pack, page 31. All alerts, timelines, and detection times in this report are drawn from DOME, Meridian's security monitoring platform.
He opened his notebook to the page where he'd copied her sticky note at twenty past six that morning, word for word, while Lou watched him do it. Check the year. Don't trust the dome.
It was 12:04. Wednesday now. He hadn't been to bed, and he didn't think he was going to.
